title: The Universe
summary: The [[milky-way|Milky Way]] is just one of many billions of galaxies. Light from distant galaxies arrives with a longer [[wavelength|wavelength]] than the same light on Earth: [[redshift|redshift]]. It shows the galaxies are moving apart, so the [[universe|Universe]] is expanding, which supports the [[big-bang-theory|Big Bang theory]]. Extended adds the microwave background, the [[hubble-constant|Hubble constant]] and the [[age-of-the-universe|age of the Universe]].

goals.text: State that our [[galaxy|galaxy]], the Milky Way, is just one of billions of galaxies in the [[universe|Universe]], and recall that it is about 100 000 [[light-year|light-years]] across.
Describe redshift, and explain why the light we receive from far-off galaxies is redshifted.
Explain how redshift shows the Universe is getting bigger, and why this backs the Big Bang theory.
Explain what the [[cosmic-microwave-background-radiation|cosmic microwave background radiation]] is and why it is now [[microwaves|microwaves]].
Describe how a [[galaxy|galaxy]]'s [[speed|speed]] and distance are measured, and use the [[hubble-constant|Hubble constant]] $H_0 = \frac{v}{d}$.
Estimate the [[age-of-the-universe|age of the Universe]] from $\frac{1}{H_0}$, and say what it suggests about where all matter began.

before.prompt: Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
before.hint: Think of the order of colours in the spectrum, from violet to red.
before.explain: Red light has the longest wavelength of visible light and violet the shortest. Beyond red come infrared, microwaves and [[radio-waves|radio waves]], with longer wavelengths still. Revise it in {{lesson:3.3}}.

before.hint: Light travels for one year. What has it covered?

options.text: a distance: how far light travels in one year
a time: how long light takes to reach the Earth
a speed: how fast light travels in one year
a brightness: how much light a star gives out in one year

before.explain: A light-year is a distance, the distance light travels through space in one year. Revise it in {{lesson:6.2.2}}.

verify.truth: a distance: how far light travels in one year

before.prompt: A cyclist rides $36\ \text{km}$ at a steady $12\ \text{km/h}$. How long does the ride take?
before.hint: Rearrange speed = distance ÷ time to find the time.
before.explain: Time = distance ÷ speed = $\frac{36}{12} = 3\ \text{h}$. Multiplying gives 432, and dividing the wrong way round gives 0.33. Revise it in {{lesson:1.2}}.

blocks.text: The Sun is one of many billions of [[star|stars]] in our [[galaxy|galaxy]], the [[milky-way|Milky Way]]. The Milky Way is huge: it is about $100\,000$ [[light-year|light-years]] across. Light would take a hundred thousand years to cross it.
Yet the Milky Way is only one galaxy. The [[universe|Universe]] contains many billions of galaxies, spread through space, each with billions of stars.

blocks.statement: Everything that exists: all of space and all the matter and energy in it, including many billions of galaxies.
blocks.plain: Everything there is, of which our galaxy is a tiny part.

blocks.question: A student writes: "The Milky Way and the Universe are two names for the same thing." Explain why the student is wrong.
steps: Say what the Milky Way is.
Say what the Universe contains, and how the two compare.
blocks.answer: The Milky Way is one galaxy, the one that contains the Sun. The Universe contains many billions of galaxies. So the Milky Way is only a tiny part of the Universe.

verify.truth: the Milky Way is one galaxy; the Universe is many billions of galaxies
forbids: the same thing as the universe
the milky way contains the universe

blocks.prompt: Which list is in order of size, smallest first?
blocks.hint: The Solar System sits inside a galaxy, and every galaxy sits inside the Universe.

options.text: the Earth, the Solar System, the Milky Way, the Universe
the Earth, the Milky Way, the Solar System, the Universe
the Earth, the Solar System, the Universe, the Milky Way
the Solar System, the Earth, the Milky Way, the Universe

blocks.explain: The Earth orbits the Sun in the Solar System. The Solar System is a tiny part of the Milky Way, and the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies in the Universe.

verify.truth: the Earth, the Solar System, the Milky Way, the Universe

blocks.prompt: One light-year is about $9.5 \times 10^{15}\ \text{m}$. Roughly how wide is the Milky Way, in metres?
blocks.hint: Multiply the width in light-years by the length of one light-year.
blocks.explain: The width is about $100\,000 = 10^{5}$ light-years, so it is $10^{5} \times 9.5 \times 10^{15} = 9.5 \times 10^{20}\ \text{m}$. Using $10\,000$ or $1\,000\,000$ light-years gives the wrong power of ten.

blocks.text: Each element gives out or absorbs light at its own set of [[wavelength|wavelengths]]. In a spectrum these show up as a pattern of lines. Scientists measure the pattern for each element here on Earth.
Light from distant galaxies shows the same patterns. But every line sits further towards red, at a longer wavelength. This is called [[redshift|redshift]].

blocks.alt: Two spectra drawn as long horizontal strips, one above the other. Each strip runs from violet, shorter wavelength, on the left to red, longer wavelength, on the right. The top strip is labelled light from a source on Earth and has three dark lines. The bottom strip is labelled light from a distant galaxy and has the same pattern of three dark lines, but each line is further to the right. Dashed lines and small arrows show each line moving to the right, towards the red end. A label reads every line shifted towards red: longer wavelength.
blocks.caption: The pattern of lines is the same, so the same elements made it. Every line has moved towards red.

blocks.statement: The stretching of electromagnetic radiation to a longer observed wavelength, because the star or galaxy that emitted it is moving away from the observer.
blocks.plain: Light from something moving away from us arrives stretched to longer wavelengths.

blocks.text: Why does it happen? When a source of [[wave|waves]] moves away from you, each [[wave|wave]] is stretched out on its way to you. You receive a longer wavelength than the source gave out. Light from stars and galaxies moving towards us would show the opposite: a shorter wavelength.

The speed of light doesn't change. So as the wavelength increases, the [[frequency|frequency]] decreases. Redshift works for all [[electromagnetic-wave|electromagnetic waves]]: each one moves towards the long-wavelength end of the [[electromagnetic-spectrum|electromagnetic spectrum]].

blocks.question: Astronomers compare the light from a distant galaxy with light from the same elements on Earth. Describe what they observe, and state what it shows about the galaxy.
steps: Say what happens to the wavelength compared with light on Earth.
Name the effect.
Say which way the galaxy is moving.
blocks.answer: Each line in the galaxy's light has a longer wavelength than the matching line measured on Earth. The whole pattern has moved towards red, so the light is redshifted. This shows the galaxy is receding: it is moving away from us.

verify.truth: observed wavelength longer than on Earth: redshift; the galaxy is moving away

blocks.prompt: Which property of light from a distant galaxy is larger when it reaches the Earth than when it was emitted?
blocks.hint: Red is at the long-wavelength end of the visible spectrum.
blocks.explain: Redshift is an increase in wavelength. The frequency goes down, and the speed of light stays the same.

blocks.prompt: Redshift can move radiation from one region of the electromagnetic spectrum into the next. Which change could redshift cause?
blocks.hint: Redshift always makes the wavelength longer.
blocks.explain: Visible light has longer wavelengths than ultraviolet, so ultraviolet can be redshifted into visible light. The other changes all go to shorter wavelengths.

blocks.text: Light from distant galaxies is redshifted whichever direction we look. So the distant galaxies are all moving away from us, and from each other. The Universe is expanding.

Picture dots drawn on a balloon. As you blow it up, every dot moves away from every other dot. No dot is the centre. The more distant galaxies also show the bigger redshift, so they are moving away faster.
Now run the expansion backwards. In the past, the galaxies were closer together. Far enough back, everything was squeezed together. This is the idea behind the [[big-bang-theory|Big Bang theory]].

blocks.statement: The theory that the Universe began billions of years ago from a single, extremely hot and dense point, and has been expanding ever since.
blocks.plain: The Universe started very small and hot, and has been getting bigger ever since.

blocks.text: Saying the Big Bang theory is about the Solar System or the Milky Way spreading out. It is the whole Universe that expands, with the galaxies moving apart.

blocks.question: What does the light reaching us from far-off galaxies tell us about the Universe? Describe the evidence.
steps: Start with the observation: compare the galaxies' light with light on Earth.
Say what redshift means for the wavelength and for the galaxies' motion.
Link it to the expansion and to the Big Bang theory.
blocks.answer: The light we receive from distant galaxies is redshifted: its observed wavelength is longer than for the same light from a source on Earth. So the galaxies are moving away from us. Galaxies in every direction are moving apart, so the Universe is expanding. This supports the Big Bang theory.

verify.truth: distant galaxies' light is redshifted (longer wavelength), so they are moving away; the Universe is expanding, supporting the Big Bang theory

blocks.prompt: Light from galaxies in every direction is redshifted. What do astronomers conclude?
blocks.hint: Redshift tells you which way a galaxy is moving relative to us.

options.text: the galaxies are moving away from each other, so the Universe is expanding
the galaxies are moving towards each other, so the Universe is shrinking
the galaxies are orbiting the Milky Way
the galaxies are made of hotter gas than the Sun

blocks.explain: A redshift means the source is moving away. Galaxies in every direction moving away means everything is spreading apart: the Universe is expanding.

verify.truth: the galaxies are moving away from each other, so the Universe is expanding

blocks.prompt: Which statement matches the Big Bang theory?
blocks.hint: Run the expansion backwards in time.

options.text: the Universe began from a single, very hot, dense point and has expanded ever since
the Solar System is spreading out into an empty Universe
the Universe has always been the same size
the Universe began as the Milky Way and the other galaxies formed later from it

blocks.explain: The galaxies are moving apart, so in the past they were closer together. In the Big Bang theory, the entire Universe began at a single point and has been expanding since.

verify.truth: the Universe began from a single, very hot, dense point and has expanded ever since

blocks.text: Point a radio telescope at any part of the sky, even where there are no stars. It still picks up faint [[microwaves|microwaves]], with almost exactly the same frequency in every direction. This is the [[cosmic-microwave-background-radiation|cosmic microwave background radiation]] (CMBR).

blocks.statement: Microwave radiation of a particular frequency that reaches us from every direction in space. It was produced shortly after the Universe formed.
blocks.plain: A faint glow of microwaves left over from the early Universe, coming from all over the sky.

blocks.text: Where does it come from? Shortly after the Big Bang, the Universe was extremely hot. It was filled with radiation of very short wavelength.

Since then the Universe has expanded hugely. The expansion has stretched this radiation, just as it stretches light from galaxies. Its wavelength has increased so much that it is now in the microwave region of the spectrum.

blocks.question: The CMBR was produced with a much shorter wavelength than microwaves. Explain why it is detected as microwaves today.
steps: Say when the radiation was produced.
Say what has happened to the Universe since then.
Say what that did to the wavelength, and where it ended up in the spectrum.
blocks.answer: The CMBR was given out very soon after the Universe began. Since then the Universe has expanded. The expansion stretched the radiation, so its wavelength increased. It is now in the microwave region of the electromagnetic spectrum.

verify.truth: produced shortly after the Universe formed; the Universe expanded, stretching it to longer wavelengths, into the microwave region
requires: very soon after the universe began

blocks.prompt: How did the wavelength of the CMBR in the early Universe compare with its wavelength today?
blocks.hint: The expansion of the Universe stretches radiation.

options.text: it was shorter than it is today
it was longer than it is today
it was the same as it is today

blocks.explain: The expansion has stretched the radiation, increasing its wavelength. So its wavelength was shorter in the past, and its frequency was higher.

verify.truth: it was shorter than it is today

blocks.prompt: Where in the sky does the CMBR come from?
blocks.hint: It was made when the whole early Universe was hot, not by any one object.

options.text: only from the direction of the Sun
only from the centre of the Milky Way
only from the most distant galaxies

blocks.explain: The CMBR fills the whole Universe, so it arrives from every direction, with almost the same frequency wherever you look.

blocks.text: To study the expansion, astronomers need two things for each galaxy: its [[speed|speed]] $v$ away from us, and its distance $d$.

Speed from redshift: astronomers measure how much the wavelength of a line in the galaxy's light has changed. The bigger the change, the faster the galaxy is moving away. You don't need the equation that turns the change into $v$.

Distance from a [[supernova|supernova]]: one kind of [[supernova|supernova]] always reaches about the same peak brightness. Astronomers compare how bright one in a far galaxy looks with how bright it really is. The dimmer it looks, the further away the galaxy.

When $v$ is plotted against $d$ for many galaxies, the points lie close to a straight line through the origin. The speed is proportional to the distance. The ratio $\frac{v}{d}$ is the [[hubble-constant|Hubble constant]], $H_0$.

blocks.statement: The speed at which a galaxy recedes from the Earth divided by its distance from the Earth.
blocks.plain: How much faster a galaxy recedes for each metre further away it is.

blocks.text: With $v$ in m/s and $d$ in m, $H_0$ is in /s (per second). Its current estimate is $2.2 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{/s}$. Rearranged, $v = H_0 d$ and $d = \frac{v}{H_0}$. On a graph of $v$ against $d$, the gradient is $H_0$.

blocks.question: The redshift of a galaxy shows it is moving away at $1.5 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m/s}$. A supernova in the galaxy shows it is $6.3 \times 10^{24}\ \text{m}$ away. Calculate a value for the Hubble constant from these measurements.
steps: Write the equation: $H_0 = \frac{v}{d}$.
Substitute, with $v$ in m/s and $d$ in m: $H_0 = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{7}}{6.3 \times 10^{24}}$.
$H_0 = 2.38 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{/s}$. Give 2 significant figures, like the data.
Check: this is close to the accepted $2.2 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{/s}$.

blocks.question: A galaxy is $1.9 \times 10^{25}\ \text{m}$ from the Earth. Take $H_0 = 2.2 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{/s}$. Calculate how fast it is receding, in km/s.
steps: Rearrange $H_0 = \frac{v}{d}$: $v = H_0 d$.
Substitute: $v = 2.2 \times 10^{-18} \times 1.9 \times 10^{25} = 4.18 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m/s}$.
Change to km/s by dividing by 1000: $v = 4.18 \times 10^{4}\ \text{km/s}$.
Round to 2 significant figures.

blocks.text: Mixing kilometres and metres. If a speed is given in km/s, change it to m/s before using $d = \frac{v}{H_0}$, or the distance comes out 1000 times too small.

blocks.prompt: A galaxy recedes from the Earth at $7700\ \text{km/s}$. Take $H_0 = 2.2 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{/s}$. How far away is it?
blocks.hint: Change the speed to m/s first, then use $d = \frac{v}{H_0}$.
blocks.explain: $v = 7.7 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m/s}$, so $d = \frac{7.7 \times 10^{6}}{2.2 \times 10^{-18}} = 3.5 \times 10^{24}\ \text{m}$. Leaving $v$ in km/s gives $10^{21}$; multiplying by $H_0$, or dividing $H_0$ by $v$, gives a tiny number.

blocks.prompt: A graph has speed of galaxy on the $y$-axis, in units of $10^{6}\ \text{m/s}$, and distance on the $x$-axis, in units of $10^{24}\ \text{m}$. The best-fit line passes through the origin and through the point $(4.0,\ 9.2)$. What value does it give for $H_0$?
blocks.hint: $H_0$ is the gradient, speed ÷ distance. Keep the powers of ten from both axes.
blocks.explain: Gradient $= \frac{9.2 \times 10^{6}}{4.0 \times 10^{24}} = 2.3 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{/s}$. Dropping the powers of ten gives 2.3, getting the sign of the power wrong gives $10^{18}$, and dividing distance by speed gives the upside-down value, $4.3 \times 10^{17}$.

blocks.text: Suppose a galaxy has always moved away at its present speed $v$. Time = distance ÷ speed, so it would have taken a time $\frac{d}{v}$ to reach distance $d$. Before that, it was in the same place as us.
Since $H_0 = \frac{v}{d}$, this time is $\frac{1}{H_0}$. It is an estimate of the [[age-of-the-universe|age of the Universe]].

Because $\frac{d}{v}$ is the same for every galaxy, they all give the same time. So every galaxy was in the same place at the same moment. This is evidence that everything in the Universe, all its matter, started at one single point.

With $H_0 = 2.2 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{/s}$, $\frac{1}{H_0}$ is about $4.5 \times 10^{17}\ \text{s}$, or about 14 billion years. It is only an estimate, because galaxies have not always moved at exactly today's speeds.

blocks.question: Use the galaxy from the first Hubble example, moving away at $1.5 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m/s}$ at a distance of $6.3 \times 10^{24}\ \text{m}$. Estimate how old the Universe is, in years.
steps: Find the seconds in one year: $365 \times 24 \times 3600 = 3.15 \times 10^{7}\ \text{s}$.
Divide to change seconds to years: $\frac{4.2 \times 10^{17}}{3.15 \times 10^{7}} = 1.33 \times 10^{10}$ years.
Round to 2 significant figures: about 13 billion years.

blocks.prompt: A different study gives $H_0 = 1.8 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{/s}$. What estimate does it give for the age of the Universe, in years? There are about $3.15 \times 10^{7}\ \text{s}$ in a year.
blocks.hint: Find $\frac{1}{H_0}$ in seconds, then divide by the seconds in a year.
blocks.explain: $\frac{1}{1.8 \times 10^{-18}} = 5.6 \times 10^{17}\ \text{s}$, and $\frac{5.6 \times 10^{17}}{3.15 \times 10^{7}} = 1.8 \times 10^{10}$ years. Leaving it in seconds gives $5.6 \times 10^{17}$; multiplying by the seconds in a year gives $1.8 \times 10^{25}$.

blocks.prompt: Why does $\frac{d}{v}$ being the same for every galaxy suggest that all matter was once at a single point?
blocks.hint: What does $\frac{d}{v}$ tell you about each galaxy's journey?

options.text: every galaxy would have started moving from the same place at the same time
every galaxy is moving at the same speed
every galaxy is the same distance from the Earth
the galaxies are moving towards a single point

blocks.explain: $\frac{d}{v}$ is how long ago a galaxy left our position. The same time for every galaxy means they all set off together from one point. Their speeds and distances differ; only the ratio is the same.

verify.truth: every galaxy would have started moving from the same place at the same time

blocks.text: Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is just one of billions of galaxies in the Universe. It measures about $100\,000$ light-years across.

Redshift: the observed wavelength of electromagnetic radiation from a receding star or galaxy is longer than the wavelength emitted. The light we receive from distant galaxies is redshifted when compared with the same light on Earth.
Distant galaxies' redshift is evidence for an expanding Universe, and supports the Big Bang theory.
The CMBR is microwave radiation arriving from every direction. It was produced shortly after the Universe formed, and the expansion has stretched it into the microwave region.

In $H_0 = \frac{v}{d}$, $v$ is the speed a galaxy moves away (found from its redshift) and $d$ is its distance (found from the brightness of a supernova in it). The current estimate is $H_0 = 2.2 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{/s}$.
$\frac{1}{H_0} = \frac{d}{v}$ estimates the age of the Universe, about 14 billion years. It is the same for every galaxy, which is evidence that all matter was once at a single point.

mistakes: Saying redshift comes from galaxies moving towards us. Redshift means the source is moving away; a source moving towards us gives a shorter wavelength.
Saying the frequency of redshifted light increases. The wavelength increases, so the frequency decreases; the speed of light stays the same.
Calling a light-year a time. It is a distance: how far light travels in one year.
Answering "the Universe began with a Big Bang" without naming redshift. The evidence is the redshift of distant galaxies, which shows they are moving away.
Extended: saying the CMBR's wavelength has decreased. The expansion has stretched it, so its wavelength has increased into the microwave region.
Extended: multiplying by the seconds in a year when changing $\frac{1}{H_0}$ from seconds to years. Divide by about $3.15 \times 10^{7}$.
examTips: To "describe" redshift, give both parts: an increase in the observed wavelength, and of light from galaxies (or stars) moving away from us.
Paper 1/2 questions often ask which region of the spectrum radiation could be shifted into. Redshift always moves it towards longer wavelengths: towards infrared, microwaves and radio waves.
Extended: to "explain" the CMBR, make separate points: it was produced shortly after the Universe formed; the Universe has expanded; its wavelength increased into the microwave region.
Extended: in $H_0 = \frac{v}{d}$ calculations, put $v$ in m/s and $d$ in m, so $H_0$ is in /s. When reading $H_0$ from a graph, use the powers of ten on both axes.
